INVESTING • RESEARCH NOTE

What happens when value investing meets momentum investing?

Can buying companies that look inexpensive while also respecting market momentum create a more balanced investment approach?

Value investing focuses on the relationship between a company's fundamentals and its market price. Momentum investing, by contrast, looks at the persistence of price trends.

Why combine them?

The two approaches can address different weaknesses. A value screen can identify businesses where expectations may already be too pessimistic, while momentum can help avoid committing capital to stocks that remain under strong selling pressure.

The important question

A combined strategy should not assume that value plus momentum automatically produces superior returns. The result depends on portfolio construction, rebalancing frequency, transaction costs, diversification and the exact definitions used for value and momentum.

This is the type of question Fiscal Frontier will test with data rather than simply assume.

VALUATION • RESEARCH NOTE

DCF: the model is only as good as the assumptions

A spreadsheet can calculate a precise number. That does not make the valuation precise.

A discounted cash flow model converts expected future cash flows into a present value. The mathematics is straightforward; the difficult part is deciding what the future cash flows, growth rate and discount rate should be.

Where judgement matters

Revenue growth, operating margins, reinvestment, terminal growth and WACC can all materially change intrinsic value. Small changes in assumptions can produce very different outputs.

Use scenarios, not false precision

A useful DCF should show what happens under optimistic, base and conservative assumptions. The objective is not to predict the future perfectly; it is to understand what expectations are embedded in today's price.

PORTFOLIO • RESEARCH NOTE

Building a portfolio around risk, not predictions

Good portfolio construction starts with accepting that the future is uncertain.

Investors often spend more time trying to predict which asset will perform best than deciding how much capital should be exposed to each outcome.

Position sizing matters

A strong investment idea can still damage a portfolio if the position is too large. Diversification and position sizing are therefore part of the investment thesis, not an afterthought.

Think in probabilities

Rather than asking only what will happen, portfolio management can ask what could happen, how damaging each scenario would be, and whether the portfolio can survive it.

EQUITY RESEARCH

How Fiscal Frontier approaches equity research

The starting point is the business, not the stock chart. I look at the company's economics, competitive position, industry structure, financial performance and management before moving toward valuation.

Financial statements, annual reports, quarterly results, investor presentations and management commentary help build the fundamental picture. Valuation then provides a framework for comparing expectations with price.

PORTFOLIO STRATEGY

Portfolio strategy is more than picking stocks

Portfolio construction brings together expected return, risk, correlation, liquidity, time horizon and position sizing. The strongest individual investments do not necessarily create the strongest portfolio when combined without considering those relationships.

Fiscal Frontier explores allocation frameworks, factor strategies, diversification and quantitative portfolio optimisation as tools for making those decisions more systematic.

QUANT • BACKTESTING

Testing an investment idea before trusting it

Backtesting allows a strategy to be evaluated against historical data. But a backtest is not proof that a strategy will work in the future.

Transaction costs, survivorship bias, look-ahead bias, position sizing and realistic execution assumptions can all change the result. Good research therefore treats backtesting as a way to challenge an idea, not as a machine for guaranteeing returns.
